job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Kira Bauer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for talking with me. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I share a flat in Leipzig with two flatmates, and my day starts with a run and then a long session at my desk. I apply for jobs in the morning, then spend the afternoon on a side project, a small app that helps tenants track repair requests. I use AI tools for nearly everything, from debugging to drafting emails. Evenings I volunteer at a repair café, fixing laptops for neighbours.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What did you study, and what was the internship?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I studied computer science at Leipzig University and finished with a good grade. My internship was eight weeks at a small logistics startup called Routeful, where I wrote tests and fixed bugs in their delivery app. They couldn't offer a job because they ran out of funding. I have about two months of savings, some student debt, and my parents in Dresden could help if I hit a wall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, nothing dramatic, and I'd be a bit disappointed because I find the technology exciting. I'd keep using the tools anyway, since even a modest gain saves me hours. Online I'd write that routine tasks get smaller and the interesting problems stay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the real obstacle is that firms have stopped hiring juniors, hype or not. I've done 60 applications since June and got four interviews. So AI isn't my problem, the job market is, and I'm a bit tired of the same standard rejection email.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep applying, maybe 15 a week, and polish my side project into something I can show. I'd put the tenant app online and see if a housing group will pilot it. I'd also pick up small freelance bug-fixing jobs on a platform to cover my rent share.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Restless more than worried. I want to be building things, and the waiting is what grinds me down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the app if no housing group wants it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd release it as open source and let people copy it. I'd rather it helps someone than sits in a folder, and a public project makes my CV look more alive than a list of grades. It might even get me noticed by a company that hires from open source.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And how long can you keep this up on your savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About two months at my current spending, maybe four if I take freelance work. After that I'd ask my parents for help, which I really don't want to do. My dad would give it without a word, and that's almost harder.

say: I'd say it's **nothing dramatic**, but the tools save me hours anyway.
Online I'd write that routine tasks shrink while the interesting problems stay.
think: Firms stopped hiring juniors, hype or not: **60 applications** since June and four interviews.
I'm tired of the same standard rejection email.
do: Send about **15 applications** a week and polish my tenant repair app.
Offer the app as a **pilot** to a housing group, or release it as open source.
Take small **freelance bug-fixing** jobs to cover my rent share.
feel: Restless more than worried, because the **waiting** is what grinds me down.

fieldNote: Her search record is concrete and is the cause of her anxiety, not AI.
Adaptive style shows in how she hedges: app, open source and freelance work in parallel.
She dislikes asking her **parents** for help, which shortens her real runway.

Offer the tenant repair app to a housing group

Use AI tools to speed up coding and cover letters

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is where my generation gets the short straw. Coding is on the card by name, and I'm a coder, so entry jobs will shrink. I'd also say it's an opportunity if people get access to the tools and training, and I'd push for that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the junior role as we know it, writing simple code and tests, goes first. Companies will want fewer people who can supervise AI output and take responsibility. That's a skill I can build, and I already work with these tools daily.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start leaning into the supervision side: reviewing AI code, writing specs, security checks. I'd finish two public projects and write about them. I'd also join a worker co-operative for tech people, which a friend started in Berlin, to find shared contracts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited and uneasy at once, like standing at the top of a slide.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a co-operative rather than a normal employer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because in a normal company the gains from AI go up, and the people who use the tools still get paid less. In a co-op we'd share both the work and the money. It's riskier and slower to start, but I like the fairness.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the co-op doesn't bring in enough to live on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd take a salaried job anywhere and keep the co-op as a side thing. I'm not too proud for that. Rent doesn't care about my principles.

say: I'd say my generation gets the **short straw**, since coding is on the card by name.
I'd also push for fair access to AI tools and training.
think: The junior role of writing simple code and tests goes first, and firms will want people who can **supervise AI**.
I can build that skill, since I already use these tools every day.
do: Practise **reviewing AI code**, writing specs and doing security checks.
Finish two public projects and write about them.
Join a **tech workers' co-operative** in Berlin for shared contracts.
feel: Excited and uneasy at once, like standing at the top of a **slide**.
S1.quote: In a normal company the gains from AI go up, and the people who use the tools still get paid less.
fieldNote: She sees both the risk and the opening, and acts on both.
Progressive values show in her choice of **co-operative** over employer, with a practical fallback.
Her anxiety is moderate: control over her skills, but income is not yet secured.

steps.text: Practise reviewing AI-written code and writing specs
Publish two projects and write about them
Join the tech workers' co-operative in Berlin
Take a salaried job and keep the co-op on the side

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we are not ready and I'd say it loudly. Two years is nothing for laws, schools or pensions. I'd tell friends to talk to their parents about money now, and I'd ask political parties what their plan is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my whole path might vanish before it starts. If AI does almost any thinking work better and cheaper within two years, no one needs a junior programmer. I tell myself robots take three more years, but that doesn't help a software person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut spending hard and take the first paying job, even if it isn't in tech, while I use the tools to build something of my own. I'd ask my parents for a rent loan and set up a small service for local shops, like automated booking. I'd also join any group that pushes for income support.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dizzy, honestly. Not sad, more like my map is being redrawn while I'm walking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd call my dad and say, I need you to understand this isn't me being lazy, the whole market is shifting. He'd probably say come home and I'd say not yet. Mum would worry more, but she'd also make soup.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any upside you'd allow yourself to see?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe cheap tools let a single person run what used to need ten. That's why I'd build the booking thing for shops. If it works, I could live from it even when companies stop hiring.

I'd ask political parties what their plan is.
think: My path might vanish before it starts, since no one needs a **junior programmer**.
Robots taking three more years doesn't help a software person.

S2.quote: I need you to understand this isn't me being lazy, the whole market is shifting.
fieldNote: She is alarmed because the entry-level coding job is exactly what she's trained for.
Even so she plans something constructive: a small business built with the same tools.
Speaks to her **dad** and mum, which shows where her support comes from.

steps.text: Take the first paying job, even outside tech
Build an automated booking service for local shops
Ask my parents for a short rent loan
Cut my monthly spending in half

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to build a safety net if we start now. I'd ask for retraining rights and a share of the profit for everyone, and I'd write to city politicians in Leipzig. I'd tell friends to learn the tools and not hide from them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm anxious but I can see ways through. If I get a job in a year, I'd have four years of experience, and I'd keep climbing toward the checking and design side. It won't be easy, but it's not hopeless.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take any tech job quickly, then pick up a security or cloud certificate, and keep the booking tool as a second income. I'd save about a quarter of my pay and keep the repair café going, because the contacts there matter. I'd also push my union to bargain about AI tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful in a restless way. I'm good at moving fast, which helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said keep the repair café. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it keeps me with people who aren't online all day. A guy named Jonas who runs it taught me soldering, and he'd tell me if my ideas were silly. Work won't be the only thing that matters if AI does it all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want your employer to promise?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That any AI tool replacing a task comes with a retraining plan for the person doing it. And that they tell us in advance, not on a Friday afternoon. It's a basic respect thing.

I'd write to Leipzig city politicians and tell friends to learn the tools.

S3.quote: Work won't be the only thing that matters if AI does it all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a chance to design a fair system instead of reacting. I'd push for a shorter work week and training rights, and I'd tell friends to learn how these systems work, not just use them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm fairly calm. A decade lets me become a real engineer with a good salary, maybe even run a small co-op. The risk is that firms use the time to quietly cut people, and then act surprised.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get a job, work up to a senior role, and study part time for a master's in AI safety. I'd keep building public tools, and I'd save for a deposit on a flat in Leipzig. I'd also stay active in local politics around tenant rights.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and curious. It feels like a long run where I can pace myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do differently in year one compared with the two-year case?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the two-year case I'd scramble. With ten years I'd choose my first job for what I'd learn, not what it pays. I might even take a smaller salary at a research lab if the mentors are good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And what about your private worries about the others?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I worry about the flatmates who aren't as comfortable with tech. Marta (my flatmate) does accounting and isn't keen on AI, and she'll have to adapt. I'd want to help her, and I'd tell the council to fund evening classes.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because I'd have no time to turn my skills into income. What would help is a basic income, fast retraining and some rent protection. I'd also want my parents to be okay, since they've never used these tools.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe whether I feel guilty using AI while I worry it takes jobs. Yes, a bit. But I'd rather understand it than stand outside it and criticise. The honest answer is that I use it daily and I'm still scared of it.

headlineQuote: I use it daily and I'm still scared of it.
